source_refs.note: Exercise 3.5, Question 17 (i), (ii): derivatives of integrals (First FTC with chain rule); book p. 103. Key on p. 300 under 'Exercise 3.2'.

blocks.explanation:
Is sawal mein integral ka derivative chahiye, jis ki upar wali limit variable \(t\) hai aur neeche wali constant \(\pi\).
Diya kya hai? Integrand \(\frac{\sin y}{1 + \sqrt{y}}\).
Find kya karna hai? \(t\) ke lihaz se derivative.
Rule kaunsa? First Fundamental Theorem (Theorem 3.2): upar wali limit ke lihaz se derivative bas integrand hai, jis mein \(y\) ki jagah \(t\) rakh dein.
Integrate karne ki koshish na karein; is integrand ka antiderivative aam functions mein hai hi nahi, aur zaroorat bhi nahi.
steps:
Diya gaya: \(F(t) = \int_{\pi}^{t} \frac{\sin y}{1 + \sqrt{y}}\,dy\).
Maloom karna: \(F'(t)\).
Tareeqa: Theorem 3.2: agar \(f\) continuous ho aur \(F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt\), to \(F'(x) = f(x)\). Derivative aur integral ek doosre ko 'cancel' kar dete hain.

Shartein check karein
\[f(y) = \dfrac{\sin y}{1 + \sqrt{y}}\ \text{is continuous for } y \geq 0\]
Kyun: \(1 + \sqrt{y}\) kam az kam 1 hai, kabhi zero nahi, aur \(\sqrt{y}\) ke liye \(y \geq 0\) chahiye. \(\pi\) positive hai, to \(t > 0\) ke liye theorem lagta hai.

First FTC lagayein
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}\int_{\pi}^{t} \dfrac{\sin y}{1 + \sqrt{y}}\,dy = \dfrac{\sin t}{1 + \sqrt{t}}\]
Kyun: upar wali limit ke lihaz se derivative = us limit par integrand. Neeche wali limit \(\pi\) constant hai, us ka koi asar nahi.
Dhyan dein: jawab \(t\) mein likhna hai; \(y\) sirf integral ke andar ka 'dummy' variable tha.

Tasdeeq
\[\int_{\pi}^{t} f(y)\,dy = G(t) - G(\pi),\quad G' = f\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}\big(G(t) - G(\pi)\big) = f(t)\]
Kyun: \(G\) koi bhi antiderivative ho, \(G(\pi)\) ek constant number hai jis ka derivative 0 hai; sirf \(G'(t) = f(t)\) bachta hai. Answer key mein bhi \(\frac{\sin t}{1 + \sqrt{t}}\) hai.

blocks.explanation:
Is dafa dono limits \(x\) par depend karti hain: neeche \(ax\) aur upar \(bx\).
Diya kya hai? Integrand \(\frac{1}{1 + t^2}\).
Find kya karna hai? \(x\) ke lihaz se derivative.
Rule kaunsa? Pehle 0 par tor kar (Property III aur II) do aise integrals banayenge jin ki sirf upar wali limit variable ho. Phir First FTC ke saath chain rule: har limit ka hissa = 'limit par integrand' times 'limit ka derivative'.
Plan: torna, har hissa differentiate, minus.
steps:
Diya gaya: \(H(x) = \int_{ax}^{bx} \frac{1}{1 + t^2}\,dt\).
Maloom karna: \(H'(x)\).
Tareeqa: Property III aur II se \(H(x) = \int_0^{bx} f - \int_0^{ax} f\); phir Theorem 3.2 chain rule ke saath: \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^{u(x)} f(t)\,dt = f(u(x))\,u'(x)\).

0 par torein
\[H(x) = \int_{0}^{bx} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2} - \int_{0}^{ax} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2}\]
Kyun: Property III se \(\int_{ax}^{bx} = \int_{ax}^{0} + \int_{0}^{bx}\), aur Property II se \(\int_{ax}^{0} = -\int_{0}^{ax}\). Ab dono integrals ki neeche wali limit constant (0) hai, jaise First FTC chahti hai.

Har hissa differentiate karein
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_{0}^{bx} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + (bx)^2} \cdot b\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_{0}^{ax} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + (ax)^2} \cdot a\]
Kyun: First FTC se upar wali limit par integrand: \(t\) ki jagah \(bx\) (ya \(ax\)). Lekin upar wali limit khud \(x\) ka function hai, is liye chain rule se us ka derivative (\(b\) ya \(a\)) multiply hota hai.
Dhyan dein: chain rule wala \(b\) aur \(a\) bhool jana sab se aam ghalti hai.

Minus karein
\[H'(x) = \dfrac{b}{1 + b^2x^2} - \dfrac{a}{1 + a^2x^2}\]
Kyun: farq ka derivative derivatives ka farq hai; \((bx)^2 = b^2x^2\).

Tasdeeq: pehle integrate kar ke
\[H(x) = \tan^{-1}(bx) - \tan^{-1}(ax)\]
\[H'(x) = \dfrac{b}{1 + b^2x^2} - \dfrac{a}{1 + a^2x^2} \;\checkmark\]
Kyun: is integrand ka antiderivative \(\tan^{-1} t\) maloom hai, to seedha \(H(x)\) nikal kar chain rule se differentiate kiya; wohi jawab. Answer key mein bhi yahi hai.
